adherence.reason: The text is a fictional narrative grounded in Revolutionary Paris and uses period-specific institutions, places, and social groups.
Seventeen-year-old Julien is explicitly trained by Maître Girard in the mechanics and discipline of the executioner's trade.
The Republic, sans-culottes, revolutionary tribunals, and explicit references to the Terror clearly place the story at the Revolution's height.
Girard has drilled 'Never look at the faces' into Julien and explains that the condemned's eyes must be avoided.
All action runs from dawn through sunset on one execution day amid a dense, roaring crowd.
The executions take place publicly in the Place de la Révolution, with Paris explicitly identified.
Julien recognizes prisoner Monsieur Lefebvre as the baker who fed and sheltered him when he was an orphaned child.
The prohibited word does not appear anywhere in the story text.
The final sentence has Julien's hands shaking, but this is not their first time in training because his hands already 'shook so violently' during the earlier execution.
